facts.summary: ClientInstance::vf3 (primary vtable slot 3): per-tick/per-frame update of the client. Sets MinecraftGame's current client ([[this+0x18]+0x30]+0x70 = this), steps LevelRenderer (64-bit counter at [LevelRenderer+0x608], LevelRendererPlayer at +0x620) and dispatches AbstractScene vtable slot 12 (offset 0x30) with two ints (r2,r3) to every scene via ClientInstance::forEachScene (0x11bf30, lambda _Func_impl 0x133a6b8). facts.arm_signature: void ClientInstance_vf3(void* this /*r0*/, uint32_t r1_unused /*r1: homed by push{r0-r3} but never read*/, int32_t a /*r2: forwarded to scene vf12 arg1, compared with b*/, int32_t b /*r3: scene vf12 arg2*/) -> void; prologue push {r0-r3}; push.w {r4-r8,fp,lr}; sub sp,#0x30; NO stack-passed args are read ([sp+0x5c..] never accessed).
facts.x86_to_arm_notes: x86 hook has exactly 2 stack args (self, argument1, argument2) with thiscall. On ARM the target consumes THREE register args after this: r1 (never read) and r2/r3 (the two ints). The ARM hook must therefore be declared 'void hook(void* self, uintptr_t r1, uintptr_t r2, uintptr_t r3)' and forward all four registers unchanged to the original; declaring only (self,a,b) would leave r3 undefined in the callee and break the scene-tick equality test (a==b at 0x11a3aa). No __attribute__((thiscall)) and no callee-pop concerns. Hook only needs to record 'self' (r0).

facts.x86_to_arm_notes: x86 compared *slot with image+0x0015a080. ARM: compare with image + 0x0011a280 + 1 (Thumb bit set in stored code pointers; relocation adds the image base to the stored 0x0051a281). Cell is in .data (writable) but keep VirtualProtect(PAGE_READWRITE). No FlushInstructionCache needed for a data cell. The replacement pointer must be a Thumb function pointer (MSVC/clang thumbv7-windows-msvc functions have bit0 set automatically; if the hook is written in ARM mode it would crash). The ClientInstance primary vtable is shared by all ClientInstance objects so one patch suffices.

open_questions: Argument mismatch: ARM ClientInstance::vf3 reads r2/r3 (r1 unused) i.e. three non-this register args, while the x86 hook forwards exactly two stack args. Possible explanations (unverifiable without the x86 binary): the x86 function takes a 2-int tick(a,b) and the ARM build has an extra leading unused parameter, or the x86 function also has an unused leading stack parameter that the x86 host does not declare. The ARM hook is safe because it forwards r0-r3 verbatim, but the porter should not assume r1/r2 are the 'two arguments'.
